Triggers.value: Beginning to feel detached or unreal

Threat.value: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

Memory.value: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.

Negative Appraisals.value: I have permanently changed for the worse
I have to be on guard all the time
I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

issues.explanation: The trigger set mixes a socially evaluative trigger ('being seen') with nonspecific discomfort/detachment, while the threat items center on danger from sudden sounds, home intrusion, and interpersonal harm. For a combat trauma profile, 'being seen' is not impossible, but here it is poorly linked to the stated threat pattern and stands out as the one trigger not plausibly connected to the strong Triggers→Threat and Triggers→Negative Appraisals edges.

issues.item: Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: Within Threat, hypervigilance to loud sounds and watching others for danger fit a combat-related threat profile, but specifically monitoring for someone entering the home implies a domestic intrusion threat context that is not supported by the triggers, memory, or appraisals. It pulls the profile toward a different trauma context and weakens cross-node coherence.

vignette: When a distant helicopter burst over the ridge that evening, Alex’s body went into a reflexive state. The sudden roar felt like a physical assault on his senses, pushing him into a state of discomfort and causing him to feel detached from the world around him. That single trigger immediately heightened his perception of threat: he heard every creak and wind whistle as a potential signal of danger, and his eyes swept over the forest canopy for any hint of movement that might signify an enemy. The acute sense of threat in those sounds also amplified his negative appraisal that the event had permanently altered him, that he was now forever on guard. In turn, that appraisal sharpened the vivid memory of the night: the smell of burning fuel lingered in his mind, the sight of smoke rising above the trees felt more real than any ordinary scene he had ever seen, and the recollection was so clear that it seemed as though he were living it again. That memory reinforced his negative appraisal, making him feel guilty for not doing more to stop the looming danger and convinced him that he could never forgive himself. Because he was constantly convinced that he had to remain hypervigilant, the very act of scanning his surroundings became a trigger in itself—each new noise or movement spurred him to look again, to check for danger, and to question whether he was truly safe. Thus, the initial trigger, the threat it produced, the memories it evoked, and the negative appraisals it nourished all fed back into one another, each element driving the next and tightening the cycle with every passing moment. Alex’s traumatic experience occurred in 2007 during a routine patrol near a remote outpost in Afghanistan. A sudden explosion blew a hole in the earth, and a helicopter from a nearby squad was brought down by shrapnel. The pilot’s screams and the smell of burning jet fuel filled the air, and Alex, then a young lieutenant, watched from a distance as the helicopter’s wreckage collapsed onto the hillside. The next day, as he returned to base, he could still smell the acrid odor whenever a distant aircraft flew overhead, and he found himself staring at the dark clouds for signs that a friendly plane might be coming or that an enemy might be hidden among them. In the months that followed, Alex’s nightly dreams were filled with the sound of rotors, and he began to dread any sudden noise in his sleep, waking up in a cold sweat whenever a lawnmower or a passing truck created a burst of sound. He avoided staying overnight at his station whenever possible, preferring to finish his duties early so that he could leave before the sun set and the forest was plunged into darkness. This avoidance grew into a pattern: he would decline night shifts and insist on being the first to leave the camp, citing fatigue and “high alertness.” His supervisor began to notice that Alex’s late departures were compromising the patrol schedule, and the tension at the ranger station mounted. He stopped attending the briefings on new navigation techniques, feeling that his thoughts were too cluttered to absorb new information. The job that had once filled him with pride and purpose now felt like a source of constant threat. Over the past year, Alex has tried to cope with the triggers that arise during his duties. Whenever he hears a helicopter or the hum of a truck engine, he instinctively scans his environment, his breathing shallow and his heart racing. He watches every employee around him, looking for any sign that someone might inadvertently or intentionally cause him harm. The more he watches, the more convinced he becomes that he is already in danger, and the stronger his belief that he has been permanently changed. Each time he feels that his body is reacting to a threat that does not exist, he feels a pang of guilt—he blames himself for not having stopped the imagined attack earlier, for failing to protect his unit. The memory of that night in Afghanistan returns vividly: the smell of burning fuel, the crackle of static on his radio, the sharp pain in his chest as he realized he could no longer escape. This memory makes his negative appraisal of “permanent damage” feel even more real, and his negative appraisal feeds back into his perception of threat, making the silence of a quiet afternoon on the trail feel as ominous as the roar of a helicopter. As a result, Alex has become a cautious, almost brittle ranger, always on the verge of collapse when a sound or a shadow catches his eye. The weight of these experiences has become so heavy that Alex finally decided to seek help. The turning point came when he missed a crucial training session because the unexpected sound of a fire alarm in the building had triggered his hypervigilant state, causing him to freeze in the doorway. When he tried to explain to his supervisor that he was "on high alert" after hearing the alarm, his boss responded with disbelief and frustration, and the confrontation left Alex feeling helpless and isolated. He realized that his avoidance and his constant state of terror were not just personal problems—they were affecting his work and his marriage. He now fears that his condition will keep him from enjoying the outdoors he loves, that it will strain his relationship with his wife, and that it might ultimately lead him to leave the park ranger job entirely. Yet he also hopes that, with help, he can reclaim the sense of safety that once made him proud of his service, and perhaps learn to trust his senses again without the constant barrage of imagined threats.
